lead: A fiber link works only if enough light reaches the receiver and the pulses are still sharp when they get there. This unit builds those two checks, the power budget and the rise-time budget, and then shows how the loss, dispersion, numerical aperture and cutoff they rest on are measured on the bench and in the field. After it you can size a point-to-point link and read an OTDR trace.
about: This unit turns the physics of fibers, sources and receivers into a design sheet. It starts with the point-to-point link and separates digital design, judged by bit error rate, from analog design, judged by carrier-to-noise ratio. The power budget then adds fiber, connector, splice and margin losses against the power the source gives and the receiver needs, and the rise-time budget checks that the pulses stay sharp, so that attenuation and dispersion each set a maximum length. The last two chapters, which only a few syllabi teach in this detail, cover the measurements behind those numbers: cut-back and OTDR attenuation, time-domain and frequency-domain dispersion, numerical aperture, cutoff wavelength, diameter, return loss and field tests.

chapters.idea: A point-to-point link is a chain of five blocks, and a digital link is judged by bit error rate while an analog link is judged by carrier-to-noise ratio.
chapters.depth: Draw the digital link: source and driver, fiber cable with splices and connectors, photodiode, preamplifier and filter, decision circuit. Name the four system considerations — bit rate, distance, received power, pulse shape. Then the analog link: same blocks, but the source is modulated linearly and the measures are carrier-to-noise ratio (CNR), distortion (composite second order, composite triple beat) and dynamic range. Define CNR = (mI)²/2 ÷ i_n², where m is the modulation index (no unit), I the mean photocurrent in amperes and i_n the RMS noise current in amperes. Close with a small table: measure used, typical target (BER 10⁻⁹ for telephony-class links), effect of noise. Descriptive only.

figure.title: The five blocks of a point-to-point link
figure.aria: Block diagram of a point-to-point link running left to right from source and driver through fiber, photodiode, preamplifier and decision circuit, ending in a bit error rate or carrier-to-noise ratio measurement.
figure.caption: Every link has these five blocks; the last block reports BER in a digital link and CNR in an analog link.

chapters.example: An analog link carries one 6 MHz video channel at 0.85 μm. The received optical power is −20 dBm, the photodiode responsivity is 0.5 A/W, the modulation index is m = 0.7, and the total RMS noise current in the 6 MHz band is 5 nA. Find the mean photocurrent, the signal current and the CNR in dB. Answer: −20 dBm = 0.01 mW, so I = 0.5 × 0.01 mW = 5 μA. Signal current = mI/√2 = 3.5/1.414 = 2.475 μA, so signal power = 6.125 μA². Noise power = (5 nA)² = (0.005 μA)² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ μA². CNR = 6.125 ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 2.45 × 10⁵ = 53.9 dB.
chapters.trap: Mixing optical power in dBm with electrical current in amperes, and forgetting that signal current is squared while noise adds as RMS.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 (sources, launching) and Unit 4 (detectors, receiver sensitivity, BER).
chapters.leave: WDM and passive components to Unit 6; loss mechanisms to Unit 2; noise derivation to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The power budget adds every loss and margin between transmitter and receiver and checks the total against the power difference available.
chapters.depth: Write P_T − P_R = αL + α_c N_c + α_s N_s + M and define each term with its unit: P_T and P_R in dBm, α in dB/km, α_c and α_s in dB, N_c and N_s as counts, M in dB. Give typical values with their wavelength: 0.2–0.25 dB/km at 1550 nm, 0.35–0.5 dB/km at 1310 nm, 2.5–3.5 dB/km at 850 nm; connector 0.5–1 dB; splice 0.1–0.2 dB; system margin 4–6 dB. Separate sensitivity (the minimum usable power) from overload (the maximum). Mention the dispersion power penalty in dB, added as one more loss term. Finish with a full case study worked line by line and the spare margin left. State the design rule: pick the cheapest source and fiber that still closes the budget.

figure.title: Walking the budget from transmitter to receiver
figure.aria: Left to right budget chain: 0 dBm launched, 1.0 dB of connectors, 13.2 dB of fiber, 0.5 dB of splices and a 6 dB margin, arriving at a receiver of −28 dBm sensitivity.
figure.caption: The four loss boxes together must stay below the 28 dB that the launched power and the sensitivity allow.

chapters.example: Design a 2.5 Gb/s point-to-point link: a 1550 nm laser with 0 dBm mean launched power, 60 km of single-mode fiber with α = 0.22 dB/km, two connectors at 0.5 dB each, one splice every 10 km at 0.1 dB each, receiver sensitivity −28 dBm at 2.5 Gb/s, and a 6 dB system margin. Does the budget close? Answer: fiber 60 × 0.22 = 13.2 dB; connectors 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 dB; splices 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 dB; margin 6 dB. Total 20.7 dB. Available power = 0 − (−28) = 28 dB. Spare margin = 28 − 20.7 = 7.3 dB. Worst-case received power = 0 − 14.7 = −14.7 dBm, which is 13.3 dB above sensitivity. The budget closes.
chapters.trap: Adding a dBm value to a dB value, or forgetting the system margin and the connector count.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the link chain; Unit 2 for loss mechanisms; Unit 3 for connector and splice losses.
chapters.leave: Rise time and dispersion limits to 5.3; measurement of α to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Loss decides how far the signal reaches and rise time decides how fast it can go; the link must pass the shorter of the two limits.
chapters.depth: Rise-time budget: T_sys = √(T_tx² + T_fiber² + T_rx²) ≤ 0.7 T_b for NRZ (0.35 T_b for RZ), with bit period T_b = 1/B and B the bit rate in bit/s. The fiber term comes from modal dispersion in multimode fiber and chromatic dispersion in single mode: T_chrom = |D| L Δλ, with D in ps/(nm·km), L in km and Δλ the RMS source spectral width in nm. Then the two limits: attenuation limit L_att = (P_T − P_R − M)/α and dispersion limit from B L |D| Δλ ≤ 1, giving L_disp = 1/(B D Δλ). Compare the two lengths; the smaller is the reach. Note that some syllabi call this the bandwidth budget, and that the 0.7 factor allows the received pulse to fill most of the bit slot without overlapping its neighbour.

figure.title: Attenuation limit and dispersion limit at 1550 nm
figure.aria: Plot of maximum link length against bit rate: a flat line at 100 km for the attenuation limit and a falling curve for the dispersion limit, crossing near 5.9 Gb/s.
figure.caption: The flat line is the loss limit of the budget, the falling curve is the dispersion limit; below the crossing loss wins, above it dispersion wins.

chapters.example: A 1 Gb/s NRZ link uses 20 km of standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm. Transmitter rise time 250 ps, receiver rise time 350 ps, source RMS spectral width 2 nm, fiber dispersion D = 17 ps/(nm·km). Does it pass? Answer: T_b = 1/B = 1 ns = 1000 ps, so the allowed system rise time is 0.7 × 1000 = 700 ps. The fiber alone may take √(700² − 250² − 350²) = √305000 = 552 ps. The actual fiber rise time is 17 × 2 × 20 = 680 ps, which is more than 552 ps, so the link fails. Maximum length = 552 ÷ (17 × 2) = 16.2 km. The loss check is easy: 20 × 0.22 = 4.4 dB, well inside a 28 dB budget, so here dispersion sets the reach.
chapters.trap: Adding rise times directly instead of root-sum-square, and using the full spectral width instead of the RMS width.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 for P_T, P_R and M; Unit 2 for chromatic and modal dispersion.
chapters.leave: Dispersion-shifted and compensating fiber design to Unit 2; measurement of D to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Attenuation is measured by the cutback method and dispersion by timing or phase across a range of wavelengths.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Cutback: measure the output power at the full length, cut back to a short length without disturbing the launch, measure again, then α = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₂) ÷ (L₁ − L₂), with powers in the same unit and lengths in km. The two-point method is its alternative name. OTDR: launch a pulse, plot backscatter against distance; the slope gives α, a step gives splice or connector loss, a reflection peak gives reflectance, and the dead zone (in m) is the blind stretch after a reflection. Dispersion, time domain (also called the pulse-delay or time-of-flight method): send short pulses at several wavelengths, measure group delay τ(λ) in ps, then D = (1/L) dτ/dλ. Dispersion, frequency domain (phase-shift method): modulate a sine wave, measure the phase shift against wavelength; this gives group delay without fast electronics. Keep it short and practical.

figure.title: Cutback measurement of attenuation
figure.aria: Vertical flow from a stable source through launch optics and the long fiber to a first power meter, then after cutting the fiber to a second power meter, ending in the attenuation calculation.
figure.caption: Source and meter stay fixed and only the fiber length changes, so P₁ and P₂ differ by loss alone.

chapters.example: A cutback measurement at 1550 nm: with 10 km of fiber in place the meter reads 200 μW; after cutting back to 2 m, with the launch untouched, it reads 1000 μW. Find α. Answer: α = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₂) ÷ (L₁ − L₂) = 10 log₁₀(1000/200) ÷ (10 − 0.002) km = 10 × 0.699 ÷ 9.998 = 0.70 dB/km. If the same fiber is measured on an OTDR, the trace slope should give the same 0.70 dB/km, which is a fair value for good single-mode fiber at 1550 nm.
chapters.trap: Dividing by the total length instead of the length difference, and letting the launch condition change when the fiber is cut.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (attenuation, chromatic dispersion); 5.2 and 5.3 for why α and D are needed.
chapters.leave: Field OTDR practice, reflectance and optical return loss to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Numerical aperture, cutoff wavelength and diameter are all read from the light that leaves the fiber, and the same instruments are used in the field.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. NA from the far-field pattern: NA = sin θ, where θ is the half-angle at which intensity falls to 5% of its peak value; also NA = √(n1² − n2²) from the index profile. Cutoff wavelength by the bend (transmission) method on a 2 m length: record output against wavelength for a straight sample and for a looped sample; the wavelength where the looped trace sits a fixed amount below the straight one is the cutoff. Diameter: core from a refracted near-field index profile, cladding from a video microscope or grey-scale image; cladding 125 μm is standard. Reflectance = 10 log₁₀(P_r/P_i), a negative dB number; optical return loss ORL = −10 log₁₀(P_r/P_i), a positive dB number. Field tests: source and power meter for installed loss, OTDR trace, visual fault locator, chromatic dispersion and PMD testers, BER test.

figure.title: Cutoff wavelength by the bend method
figure.aria: Plot of relative output against wavelength: a flat straight-fiber trace at 0 dB and a looped-fiber trace that falls steeply below about 1200 nm.
figure.caption: Below cutoff the loop strips light from the cladding, so the looped trace drops away; near 1200 nm the gap reaches the 0.1 dB the standard asks for.

chapters.example: A step-index fiber has n1 = 1.46. In the far field the intensity falls to 5% of its peak at a half-angle of 12° from the axis. Find the numerical aperture, the acceptance angle in air and n2. Answer: NA = sin 12° = 0.208. Measured in air, the acceptance angle equals this half-angle, so θ_a = 12°. Then n2 = √(n1² − NA²) = √(1.46² − 0.208²) = √(2.1316 − 0.0433) = √2.0883 = 1.445. A larger half-angle would mean a higher NA; the 5% level, not the 50% level, is what the far-field definition uses.
chapters.trap: Calling the operating wavelength the cutoff wavelength, and giving reflectance and ORL the wrong sign.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (numerical aperture, cutoff wavelength); 5.4 for the measurement bench.
chapters.leave: PMD measurement and dispersion compensation to Unit 2 and Unit 6; connector reflectance design to Unit 3.

links: the transmitted power and the receiver sensitivity become the two ends of the budget
the budget fixes distance by loss, the rise-time budget fixes it by bit rate
the bit rate set in the link chain fixes the allowed system rise time
the budgets assume α and D, which are then measured
the same source-and-power-meter bench measures NA and cutoff
field loss tests confirm the installed budget still holds
